content.summary: Welcome to your final reading mission in level A2. In this module, you will learn how to read and understand extended reading passages where writers share opinions, explain reasons with examples, and use natural conversational phrases. You will discover how to build longer answers and connect your thoughts smoothly, bridging the gap toward B1 intermediate English.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Extended response patterns using Point, Reason, and Example structures, plus conversational discourse markers.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Advanced descriptive words for expressing opinions, personal views, and spontaneous reactions.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Identifying text structure, recognizing discourse markers for transitions, and following author arguments.

learningObjectives: Understand the structure of extended reading passages with reasons and examples.
Recognize discourse markers that introduce opinions and transitions in text.
Identify key details and author perspectives in short opinion articles.

contextWarmup.prompt: When someone asks you an unexpected question in English, what is the best way to start your answer?
options: Say nothing and stay completely silent.
Use a thinking phrase like 'Let me think...' or 'Well...', then give your point.
Change the subject immediately to something else.
contextWarmup.explanation: Using a thinking phrase gives you a moment to gather your thoughts and helps your speech flow naturally before you state your point.

rules: Rule 1: Build extended responses by stating a clear point, giving a reason, and sharing a personal example.
Rule 2: Use discourse markers such as 'actually', 'frankly', and 'well' to add natural transitions and sound more conversational.
Rule 3: When reading opinion texts, look for transition words that show the author changing direction or adding a new perspective.

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often stop after saying just yes or no, missing the chance to explain why or provide an example.
commonTrap.wrong: Do you like travel? Yes, I do.
commonTrap.correct: Yes, I love travel. It changes my perspective because you see new cultures. For instance, my trip to Bali was fascinating.

paragraphs: Many language learners find it difficult to give spontaneous answers when someone asks an unexpected question. Initially, you might feel nervous and stay silent. However, building extended responses is much easier if you follow a simple structure. First, state your point clearly. Next, explain your reason. Finally, give a short personal example from your daily life.

For instance, if a friend asks about your favorite hobby, do not just say reading. Frankly, you should say that reading is your favorite activity because it expands your perspective. You can add that last month you read a fascinating book about nature. Using discourse markers like well or actually also helps your speech flow smoothly and gives you time to think.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Spontaneous Fluency & Extended Responses

content.summary: Practical guide on building extended sentences, using discourse markers, and structuring paragraphs with points, reasons, and examples in English.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Point, Reason, and Example Structure
blueprintItems.example: I prefer working online. It saves time because I do not commute. For instance, I save one hour every morning.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Using Discourse Markers
blueprintItems.example: Actually, I think learning languages is fun because you can talk to people from different countries.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Handling Unexpected Questions
blueprintItems.formula: Thinking Filler + Direct Answer + Supporting Detail
blueprintItems.example: That is an interesting question. I would choose the mountains because I enjoy hiking in fresh air.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always place a comma after introductory discourse markers like Actually, Well, or Honestly.
mechanicsRules.why: Introductory words need a comma to separate them from the main clause.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize the first letter of every new sentence and proper noun.
mechanicsRules.badExample: i like london because it is historic.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I like London because it is historic.
mechanicsRules.why: Sentences and city names require capital letters in English.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use correct conjunctions to connect reasons and examples smoothly.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I like sports for instance I play tennis every weekend.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I like sports. For instance, I play tennis every weekend.
mechanicsRules.why: Independent clauses need proper punctuation or a transition phrase when connecting ideas.

guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three or four sentences about your favorite season. Mention what it is, give a reason using because, and provide an example.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Answer an Unexpected Question
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write a response to an unexpected question about whether city life is better than country life. Use a thinking filler and give an extended response with a reason and example.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Expand this simple sentence into an extended response with a point, reason, and example:

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Spontaneous Fluency & Extended Responses

content.summary: As you move from A2 to B1, speaking becomes more spontaneous and less rehearsed. Learn how to connect your ideas, use conversational fillers naturally, and give extended responses with clear reasons.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on linking words together and maintaining a steady rhythm. Avoid long silent pauses by using natural phrases like well, I suppose or frankly speaking.

pillars.name: Vowel Clarity
pillars.explanation: Pronounce every vowel sound distinctly, especially when speaking quickly or expressing spontaneous ideas.

pillars.name: Connected Speech
pillars.explanation: Connect the end of one word to the beginning of the next word to sound natural and fluent.

pillars.name: Extended Answers
pillars.explanation: Do not stop after one short sentence. Always add a reason and an example to expand your speaking turn.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how the main stress shifts as the word form changes.
The stress stays firmly on the second syllable for plural forms.
Adjectives often place stress on the first syllable, while verbs shift the stress.
The stress remains on the first syllable in both noun and adjective forms.
